title: The Story of Money · Episode 3
chapters: The gold standard and the end of Bretton Woods
Quantitative easing: what central banks do when rates hit zero

units.t: The Story of Money. Episode three.
In this episode: The gold standard and the end of Bretton Woods, The global financial crisis of 2008 and Quantitative easing: what central banks do when rates hit zero.
Part one. The gold standard and the end of Bretton Woods.
For generations, money was promised to be as good as gold.
Then on a Sunday night in 1971, an American president broke the link with a television address.
Money tied to metal.
Under the gold standard a government promised that its paper money could be exchanged for a fixed weight of gold on demand.
Britain led the way.
The pound was effectively linked to gold from the early 1700s, partly through a gold price set in 1717 while Isaac Newton was Master of the Mint, and formally from 1821.
By the 1870s Germany, the United States and many others had joined.
Because each currency was fixed to gold, they were fixed to each other, making trade and lending more predictable.
Governments could not simply print money, so long-run inflation stayed low.
The classical gold standard lasted until the First World War.
The golden straitjacket.
The discipline came at a cost.
The money supply depended on how much gold a country held, not on what the economy needed.
When gold flowed out, a country often had to raise interest rates and squeeze its economy, even in a slump.
Prices could fall for years, making debts harder to repay.
The system also depended on new gold discoveries.
Gold rushes in California, Australia and South Africa expanded the world's money supply in ways that had nothing to do with economic policy.
Gold and the Depression.
After the First World War, countries tried to rebuild the gold standard.
In 1925 Britain, with Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, returned to gold at the pre-war rate, which most economists now agree overvalued the pound and hurt British industry.
John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a pamphlet called The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill.
When the Great Depression struck, the gold standard helped spread deflation from country to country, as central banks raised rates to defend their gold.
Britain left gold in 1931 and the United States effectively devalued in 1933.
Research by economic historians, including Barry Eichengreen and Ben Bernanke, found that countries leaving gold earlier tended to recover faster.
Bretton Woods and Triffin.
In July 1944, delegates from 44 Allied nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, led by Keynes for Britain and Harry Dexter White for the United States.
Other currencies were pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar was convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce, but only for foreign governments and central banks.
The conference also created the IMF and what became the World Bank.
Around 1960, economist Robert Triffin spotted a hidden contradiction.
The world needed a growing supply of dollars for trade, which came from American spending abroad.
But the more dollars piled up overseas, the less likely America held enough gold to honour them.
Vietnam war spending widened the gap, and France under de Gaulle began converting dollars into gold.
The Nixon shock.
On Sunday 15 August 1971, President Richard Nixon went on television and announced that the United States would temporarily stop converting dollars into gold for foreign governments.
He also imposed wage and price controls and a surcharge on imports.
The suspension was never lifted.
Attempts to patch together new fixed rates collapsed, and by 1973 the major currencies were floating against each other.
Since then, the world's money has been fiat money, valuable because governments declare it legal tender and people trust it, not because it can be exchanged for metal.
Some still call for a return to gold, but most economists argue that flexibility in crises is worth the loss of the golden anchor.
The key idea: Under the gold standard a currency could be swapped for a fixed amount of gold, which kept inflation low but tied governments' hands.
Part two. The global financial crisis of 2008.
It began with American home loans that should never have been made.
Within months, some of the world's biggest banks were failing and governments were scrambling to stop a second Great Depression.
A boom built on credit.
In the early 2000s American house prices rose rapidly for years.
Interest rates were low after the dot-com crash, and lenders competed fiercely for business.
Many began offering subprime mortgages to borrowers with weak credit histories, sometimes with little checking of income at all, and often with low introductory rates that would jump later.
The thinking was that rising house prices would bail everyone out: a struggling borrower could refinance or sell at a profit.
Buyers, lenders and investors all assumed prices would keep climbing, or at least would not fall across the whole country at once.
When prices peaked around 2006 and began to fall, that assumption collapsed, and defaults began to climb.
Hidden risk and leverage.
Many lenders did not keep the loans they made.
Banks bundled thousands of mortgages into securities and sold them to investors, a process called securitisation.
These were repackaged into more complex products, such as collateralised debt obligations, which split the income into layers of risk.
Rating agencies gave many top layers their highest AAA rating.
Pension funds, banks and councils worldwide bought them.
Lenders who could sell loans on had less reason to care whether borrowers could repay, and few investors understood where the risk sat.
Leverage magnified the danger.
Many investment banks borrowed around thirty dollars or more for every dollar of their own capital, much of it short term.
A small fall in asset values could wipe them out.
September 2008.
In March 2008 the investment bank Bear Stearns was rescued through a sale to JPMorgan Chase, with support from the US Federal Reserve.
Then, in September, the authorities chose not to rescue Lehman Brothers, a 158-year-old investment bank.
On 15 September it filed for bankruptcy, the largest in US history, with assets of more than 600 billion dollars.
Within days the insurer AIG, which had sold huge amounts of protection against mortgage defaults, needed a massive government rescue.
A large money market fund that held Lehman debt ‘broke the buck’, sparking runs on similar funds.
Lending between banks almost seized up, and share markets plunged.
Governments responded with unprecedented measures, including the 700 billion dollar US rescue program known as TARP.
How Australia dodged recession.
Australia came through better than almost any other advanced economy.
Its big banks had less exposure to American subprime securities and were closely supervised.
The Reserve Bank cut the cash rate from 7.
25 per cent in September 2008 to 3 per cent by April 2009.
The government guaranteed bank deposits and wholesale funding, and spent heavily on stimulus, including cash payments to households and a large school building program.
Meanwhile China launched its own enormous stimulus, keeping demand for Australian iron ore and coal strong.
The economy shrank in only one quarter, at the end of 2008, so it avoided the technical definition of a recession: two consecutive quarters of decline.
The long shadow.
Elsewhere, the damage lasted years.
Millions of Americans lost their homes, US unemployment reached around 10 per cent, and parts of Europe slid into a debt crisis from 2010, with Greece the most severe case.
Central banks cut interest rates to near zero and bought bonds on a vast scale.
Regulators responded with new rules.
The international Basel III standards required banks to hold more and better quality capital and more liquid assets, and the US passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010.
Debate continues over whether the reforms went far enough, and over the fairness of rescuing banks while many ordinary people bore the costs.
The crisis also fuelled lasting public anger at finance.
The key idea: In the early 2000s, easy loans to risky borrowers drove US house prices up, on the assumption they would keep rising.
Part three. Quantitative easing: what central banks do when rates hit zero.
When interest rates can fall no further, central banks reach for a stranger tool: creating money to buy bonds.
Australia tried it in 2020, with mixed results.
The zero lower bound.
Normally the Reserve Bank of Australia steers the economy with its cash rate, the overnight rate at which banks lend to each other.
Cutting it makes borrowing cheaper and encourages spending and investment.
But there is a floor.
Near zero, further cuts become difficult, because people and banks could simply hold cash, which pays nothing but never charges you either.
Economists call this the zero lower bound.
A few central banks in Europe and Japan pushed rates slightly negative, but not by much.
When a severe downturn hits and rates are already near zero, central banks need another tool.
The best known is quantitative easing, or QE.
How QE works.
Under QE, a central bank buys large amounts of financial assets, mainly government bonds, from banks and investors.
It pays with newly created reserves: electronic money in the accounts that commercial banks hold at the central bank.
Despite the popular phrase, no banknotes are printed.
The buying pushes bond prices up, and because prices and yields move in opposite directions, longer-term interest rates fall.
That feeds through to mortgages and business loans.
Sellers also receive cash they may put into corporate bonds or shares, an effect called portfolio rebalancing.
QE also signals that the bank intends to keep rates low for a long time.
From Tokyo to the world.
Japan tried modern QE first.
After its asset bubble burst in the early 1990s, it endured years of weak growth and falling prices.
From 2001 to 2006 the Bank of Japan bought government bonds to expand bank reserves, and it later revived the approach on a far larger scale.
The 2008 financial crisis made QE mainstream.
The US Federal Reserve bought trillions of dollars of bonds and mortgage-backed securities, the Bank of England began in 2009 and the European Central Bank in 2015.
Related tools exist too.
The Fed capped bond yields from the Second World War until 1951, and the Bank of Japan adopted a version in 2016.
Australia's 2020 experiment.
Australia skipped QE in the global financial crisis because its rates were well above zero.
The pandemic changed that.
In March 2020 the RBA cut the cash rate to 0.
25 per cent, set the same target for three-year government bond yields and offered banks cheap funding.
In November 2020 it cut both to 0.
1 per cent and began a $100 billion Bond Purchase Program, later extended to roughly $280 billion in total.
The yield target ended badly.
In 2021 the recovery was faster than expected and inflation rose, so markets bet on earlier rate rises than the bank's guidance of low rates until 2024.
The RBA abandoned the target in November 2021, and later reviews acknowledged the disorderly exit damaged its credibility.
Did it work.
Most central bank research finds QE lowered long-term interest rates and helped steady markets in crises.
Its effect on jobs and growth is much harder to measure, because nobody can rerun history without it.
Critics raise three concerns.
By lifting the prices of bonds, shares and property, QE may have widened wealth gaps, since wealthier people own most of those assets.
It can blur the line between monetary policy and government financing.
And when rates later rose, central banks faced large losses on the bonds they held.
The RBA has reported negative equity as a result, though central banks can keep operating normally in that situation.
The key idea: Central banks steer the economy with interest rates, but cutting them stops working once they approach zero.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Under a gold standard, what could you do with paper money?
Answer. Exchange it for a fixed amount of gold.
Question two. What were subprime mortgages?
Answer. Home loans to weak-credit borrowers.
Question three. Why do central banks struggle to cut interest rates much below zero?
Answer. Holding cash pays nothing but costs nothing.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
